newsitem.title: USA: Local labor mkt tight, nearing limits -- Minn. Fed.
newsitem.headline: Local labor mkt tight, nearing limits -- Minn. Fed.

text.p: Labor markets in the ninth U.S. economic district are extremely tight, and any further employment gains may spark inflationary wage pressures, said an official at the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis.
"In our area, our labor markets continue to be very tight ... That's almost across-the-board," Edward Lotterman, regional economist at the Minneapolis Fed, told Reuters.

Lotterman said local businessmen told Minneapolis Fed head Gary Stern in a recent meeting that keeping and securing workers was their number one problem at this stage of the U.S. economic expansion, which has embarked on its seventh year.

The continued job tightness in the ninth district suggests that a possible slackening in the national employment market -- as hinted by a rise in the June jobless rate to 5.0 percent -- may not be evenly distributed across the nation.
The ninth region covered by the Minneapolis Fed includes Minnesota, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, 26 counties in northwestern Wisconsin and the Upper Peninsula of Michigan.
Lotterman said the level of firmness in the regional job market suggests that further gains were likely to be limited.
"We see a very tight labor market. We've seen pretty good employment growth, but I think it's limited. We've sort of sopped up everybody who's available," he said.
Does that mean higher wage pressures ahead?

"We are at the point in this district where we are not likely to have further increases in employment ... without seeing pressure on wages that will eventually translate through into some pressures on prices," Lotterman said.

"Not necessarily huge price increases, but there will be some increases at the margin ... it may be enough to bump the price indices up a point or two more than they went up, say, last year," he added.

The Minneapolis Fed economist said some incipient labor cost pressures had already been detected. Not so much on higher salaries, he said, but also on compensation and benefit costs and incentives such as signing bonuses, among others.
Despite the jitters, however, none or very little of these pressures have been actually translated into higher price tags for the consumer in the ninth district.
"It's correct to say we don't see any signs of inflation in terms of prices of goods and services," Lotterman said.
But the positive labor conditions are likely to continue to foster consumer spending in the region. Lotterman said local spending has been flourishing for some time.

"Spending has been pretty robust and it isn't always on the same things ... We're seeing pretty good sales, consumer purchases and I think our expectations are that that's likely to continue at least for some time," he said.
